title: SAM 3D Animal: Promptable Animal 3D Reconstruction from Images in the Wild
claim: Our method reconstructs every instance in a crowded, occluded multi-subject scene jointly from a single image.
layout: 2 panels side by side, input left, overlaid reconstruction right
description: Two equal-sized panels sit side by side. The left panel is a classical oil painting of a pastoral scene: ruined stone arches in the background, a gnarled tree on the left, and two shepherds resting on a rock at the right. A crowded herd of cows, sheep, goats and dogs fills the foreground, and many of them overlap. The right panel is the same painting with each animal covered by a smooth, pale-white untextured 3D mesh. The meshes match each animal's pose, size and species and keep their separate identities despite occlusion. The shepherds and background are left unchanged. The eye goes first to the white meshes, which stand out against the warm, muted painting. There is no text, arrows or labels.
caption: A promptable view of multi-animal 3D reconstruction. We present SAM 3D Animal, a promptable framework that addresses the problem of joint 3D reconstruction of multiple animals from a single image. Here, we show the input image together with the overlay reconstruction results.
abstract: 3D animal reconstruction in the wild remains challenging due to large species variation, frequent occlusions, and the prevalence of multi-animal scenes, while existing methods predominantly focus on single-animal settings. We present SAM 3D Animal, the first promptable framework for multi-animal 3D reconstruction from a single image. Built on the SMAL+ parametric animal model, our method jointly reconstructs multiple instances and supports flexible prompts in the form of keypoints and masks which enable more reliable disambiguation in crowded and occluded scenes. To train such a model, we further introduce Herd3D, a multi-animal 3D dataset containing over 5K images, designed to increase diversity in species, interactions, and occlusion patterns. Experiments on the Animal3D, APTv2, and Animal Kingdom datasets show that our framework achieves state-of-the-art results over both existing model-based and model-free methods, demonstrating a scalable and effective solution for prompt-driven animal 3D reconstruction in the wild.
